claim: Intelligence and education are predictive of better physical and mental health, socioeconomic position (SEP), and longevity.
source: Intelligence and education are predictive of better physical and mental health, socioeconomic position (SEP), and longevity.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Intelligence and education are phenotypically and genetically correlated.
source: Intelligence and education are phenotypically and genetically correlated, which makes it difficult to elucidate causal relationships.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research in the introduction.

claim: Higher intelligence had positive direct effects on income and alcohol consumption.
source: Higher intelligence had positive direct effects on income and alcohol consumption, and negative direct effects on moderate and vigorous physical activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Higher intelligence had negative direct effects on moderate and vigorous physical activity.
source: Higher intelligence had positive direct effects on income and alcohol consumption, and negative direct effects on moderate and vigorous physical activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Higher educational attainment had positive direct effects on income, alcohol consumption, and vigorous physical activity.
source: Higher educational attainment had positive direct effects on income, alcohol consumption, and vigorous physical activity, and negative direct effects on smoking, BMI and sedentary behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Higher educational attainment had negative direct effects on smoking, BMI and sedentary behaviour.
source: Higher educational attainment had positive direct effects on income, alcohol consumption, and vigorous physical activity, and negative direct effects on smoking, BMI and sedentary behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Children who score more highly in intelligence tests tend to remain in school for longer.
source: On average, children who score more highly in intelligence tests tend to remain in school for longer, (Deary et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Deary et al., 2007.

claim: People who remained in school for longer tend to have higher intelligence later in life.
source: people who remained in school for longer tend to have higher intelligence later in life (Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018.

claim: Intelligence and educational attainment are partially heritable.
source: Intelligence and educational attainment are partially heritable, and strongly genetically correlated (rg=0.70) (Lee et al., 2018; Hill et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2016b; Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published GWAS studies.

claim: Intelligence and educational attainment are strongly genetically correlated (rg=0.70).
source: Intelligence and educational attainment are partially heritable, and strongly genetically correlated (rg=0.70) (Lee et al., 2018; Hill et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2016b; Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement provides a specific genetic correlation estimate supported by citations.

claim: A review found some evidence that increases in education led to lower mortality, especially for older cohorts.
source: A review of the effects of educational attainment on socio-economic and health outcomes in later life found some evidence that increases in education led to lower mortality, especially for older cohorts (Galama et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Galama et al., 2018.

claim: There was little consistent evidence of effects of education on obesity.
source: However, there was little consistent evidence of effects on other outcomes such as obesity (Galama et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Galama et al., 2018.

claim: Each year of education causes measured IQ to increase by on average 1 to 5 points.
source: A systematic review of 28 studies provided evidence using quasi-experiential designs that each year of education causes measured IQ to increase by on average 1 to 5 points (Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a systematic review.

claim: Intelligence test scores taken at age 11 strongly associate with educational attainment later in life.
source: Large prospective studies have found that intelligence test scores taken at age 11 strongly associate with educational attainment later in life, a link that is, in part, explained by shared genetic effects (Deary et al., 2007; Calvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prospective studies.

claim: The link between intelligence at age 11 and educational attainment is, in part, explained by shared genetic effects.
source: Large prospective studies have found that intelligence test scores taken at age 11 strongly associate with educational attainment later in life, a link that is, in part, explained by shared genetic effects (Deary et al., 2007; Calvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prospective studies.

claim: There are no quasi-experimental studies of the effects of intelligence on education.
source: However, there are no quasi-experimental studies of the effects of intelligence on education because intelligence is less subject to perturbation by natural experiments such as policy reforms.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of a type of study, with reasoning provided.

claim: Intelligence is less subject to perturbation by natural experiments such as policy reforms.
source: However, there are no quasi-experimental studies of the effects of intelligence on education because intelligence is less subject to perturbation by natural experiments such as policy reforms.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining why certain studies don't exist.

claim: At each SNP, offspring inherit at random one of their mother's two possible alleles and one of their father's two possible alleles.
source: At each SNP, offspring inherit at random one of their mother's two possible alleles and one of their father's two possible alleles.
evidence: This is a statement about Mendelian inheritance, which is established genetic knowledge.

claim: With the exception of somatic mutation, SNPs are invariant post-conception.
source: With the exception of somatic mutation, SNPs are invariant post-conception, so it is not possible for the environment or developing disease to affect inherited DNA.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of SNPs, which is established genetic knowledge.

claim: It is not possible for the environment or developing disease to affect inherited DNA.
source: With the exception of somatic mutation, SNPs are invariant post-conception, so it is not possible for the environment or developing disease to affect inherited DNA.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of inherited DNA, which is established genetic knowledge.

claim: SNPs are not affected by reverse causation.
source: Thus, SNPs are not affected by reverse causation, which can distort causal interpretations of observational epidemiological associations.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of Mendelian randomization based on genetic knowledge.

claim: Genetic variants are largely unrelated to factors that would confound conventional observational studies.
source: Segregation of alleles at germ cell formation (Mendel's first law) and the independent assortment of alleles with respect to the rest of the genome excepting proximal DNA segments (Mendel's second law), and the lack of environmentally influenced effects on survival from conception through to live birth and study entry, leads to genetic variants being largely unrelated to factors that would confound conventional observational studies (Davey Smith, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and is based on Mendelian principles.

claim: SNPs that affect intelligence are likely to also affect education and vice versa.
source: However, this could be misleading, as SNPs that affect intelligence are likely to also affect education and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known correlation between intelligence and education.

claim: The SNPs associated with intelligence and education are pleiotropic – and most affect both traits.
source: Thus, the SNPs associated with intelligence and education are pleiotropic – and most affect both traits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic correlation between intelligence and education.
